title: Traversal, Counting and Searching: Walking from head
quickIdea: Every list operation begins with the same walk: a pointer starts at head and follows next until it reaches the node you want or hits NULL, which costs O(n) time.
remember: The standard loop is for (p = head; p != NULL; p = p->next) visit(p);. Its body runs exactly n times for n nodes.
Test p, not p->next, unless the body needs the successor. A loop written while (p->next != NULL) stops one node early, and a body that dereferences p->next->next on the last node dereferences NULL.

Counting nodes and searching for a key are both Theta(n). In the worst case the key is absent or last, so n comparisons are needed; a binary search is impossible because the list has no O(1) midpoint.
Recursion over a list uses one frame per node. For a non-empty list, size(head) = 1 if head->next == NULL, else 1 + size(head->next); the depth equals n.
A pairwise walk uses two pointers: p = q->next; q = p ? p->next : 0; advances two nodes per iteration, which lets a swap of adjacent values touch each node once.
The traversal must be restarted from head for every new search. Nothing is cached, and there is no way to resume a walk from a node you no longer hold.

example.prompt: GATE CSE 2008 Q.62. The list holds 1,2,3,4,5,6,7. The function swaps p->value with q->value, then sets p = q->next and q = p ? p->next : 0, with p starting at the first node and q at the second. What is the list afterwards?
example.work: Round 1 swaps nodes 1 and 2, giving 2,1,3,4,5,6,7, then moves p to node 3 and q to node 4. Round 2 gives 2,1,4,3,5,6,7 and moves p to node 5, q to node 6. Round 3 gives 2,1,4,3,6,5,7 and moves p to node 7; q becomes p->next, which is NULL, so the loop ends.
example.answer: 2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5, 7. The seventh value is untouched because the loop pairs nodes two at a time.

gateAngle: Traces are the cheapest marks in this topic. GATE CSE 2008 Q.62 pairs adjacent values, GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 asks for the base case and the recursive step of a node count, and GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 hides a deletion inside a walk. In each case you write the pointer values after every iteration instead of guessing the final list.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2026 Set 1. getListSize(head) returns 1 if E1, else returns E2, for a non-empty singly linked list. Which E1 and E2 count the nodes?
variations.answer: E1: head->next == NULL and E2: 1 + getListSize(head->next).
variations.why: The list is guaranteed non-empty, so the base case is the single-node list, whose next is NULL. The recursive step must advance to head->next; calling getListSize(head) again never reaches the base case.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A list of 5 nodes is searched for a key that is not present. How many comparisons are made, and how many would a sorted array of 5 elements need in the worst case?
variations.answer: 5 comparisons for the list; 3 for the sorted array.
variations.why: The list must visit every node to be sure the key is absent, so the cost is n. Binary search on 5 sorted elements compares against the middle and then at most two more, which is ceil(log2(6)) = 3.

trap.what: Advancing the pointer after a deletion inside the same loop, or writing the loop test as p->next != NULL and then reading p->next->next.
trap.why: After you unlink the node after p, p already points at the following node, so p = p->next skips one. And on the last node p->next is NULL, so p->next->next dereferences NULL.
trap.counterexample: Delete every node after the head from 1,2,3,4 using if (found) p->next = p->next->next; else p = p->next;. Advancing in both branches visits 2 and 4 but never 3, leaving 3 in the list. GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 is built on exactly this distinction.

check.question: In the loop while (p->next != NULL) { p = p->next; } starting at head of a 4-node list, where does p finish and how many times does the body run?
check.answer: p finishes on the last node and the body runs 3 times.
check.explanation: The loop stops when p->next is NULL, which is true only at the tail. That is the correct way to reach the last node, and the wrong way to visit every node, which is why the condition must be chosen from the body's needs.
